They tolerate cold and stay active around 15 C, surviving near 5 C; luggage travel enables spread across routes, including China and Europe. In hotels, inspect sheets and room corners for dark spots (feces) or dead insects; after travel, wash washable items and air-dry belongings, leaving non-washables outside if possible. Bed bugs do not transmit diseases, but infestations can be disruptive. Ticks are increasingly found in urban green spaces, parks, lawns, and city flowerbeds. articleSummary: As of 13 August 2026, Delhi reports 1,344 H1N1 influenza A cases this season, highlighting how influenza can mimic a common cold yet progress rapidly. H1N1 typically presents with sudden onset of fever, dry cough, severe body aches, headache, sore throat, chills and marked fatigue, sometimes accompanied by vomiting or diarrhoea in children; a high-grade fever and diffuse aches contrast with the gradual onset and milder symptoms of a common cold, which more commonly features sneezing, runny nose and congestion with little or no fever. Nevertheless, symptom overlap means diagnosis is clinical, not definitive without testing. High-risk groups include pregnant women, older adults, young children, diabetes, chronic kidney/heart/lung disease, immune compromise and obesity. Seek medical attention for severe, worsening, or at-risk individuals; urgent care is advised for breathlessness, chest pain, persistent fever, confusion, blue lips or hypoxia, or deterioration after initial improvement during active influenza.

articleSummary: New Delhi outlines Dengue and H1N1 Swine Flu, emphasizing distinct transmission with overlapping febrile, pain-related symptoms. Dengue, spread by Aedes mosquitoes, presents with sudden high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, muscle and joint aches, nausea/vomiting, fatigue, and a red rash; some patients have swollen glands. Symptoms usually appear 4–10 days after infection. Alarm features include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from nose or gums, rapid breathing, extreme weakness, or blood in vomit or stool, requiring urgent care. H1N1 influenza, transmitted via respiratory droplets, causes abrupt fever, dry cough, sore throat, headache, chills, body pains, runny nose, and fatigue; vomiting/diarrhea can occur, and pneumonia or breathing difficulty may develop in severe cases. Diagnosis relies on medical evaluation: dengue blood tests; influenza tests as indicated. Prevention: eliminate standing water to curb dengue; for H1N1, hand hygiene, masking, cough etiquette, distancing, and vaccination per clinician advice. Seek medical testing for accurate diagnosis based on symptoms.

articleSummary: Bromhexine hydrochloride is proposed as a host-directed prophylactic against COVID-19 and influenza by inhibiting TMPRSS2, aiming for Pharmacologically Attenuated Natural Immunization (PANI), which would reduce viral entry and early replication while preserving antigen exposure to generate immune memory. The concept paper by Vanyo Mitev of the Medical University-Sofia, Bulgaria, notes observations across elderly individuals and a child taking bromhexine, including a 72-year-old man in Thailand who used 8 mg twice daily for ~2 weeks before SARS-CoV-2 infection; his illness was almost silent, with anti-spike antibodies reaching 2,080 BAU/mL around 3 months and remaining high ~9 months later. His 71-year-old wife, also prophylaxed, remained asymptomatic and had 1,040 BAU/mL at ~3 months with antibodies persisting. An eight-year-old child and other bromhexine users with comorbidities showed attenuated disease. The study, not peer-reviewed and published on Preprints.org, calls for randomized trials to confirm efficacy against COVID-19 and influenza and to measure viral loads.

articleHeadline: New Bundibugyo Virus Variant Emerges in Congo-Uganda Ebola Outbreak
articleSummary: Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) caused a 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. Genomic analysis of 22 BDBV genomes from DRC and Uganda (21 high-quality) shows the 2026 viruses form a distinct cluster separate from lineages of the 2007–2008 Uganda outbreak and the 2012 DRC outbreak, indicating a new animal-to-human spillover rather than reintroduction from earlier BDBV lineages. Cross-border transmission occurred, with Ugandan cases linked to a single transmission chain rather than multiple introductions. The 2026 cluster harbors 25 mutations, including nine with patterns consistent with ADAR-mediated RNA editing and five that alter viral proteins. Diagnostic tests were imperfect: some samples tested negative on GeneXpert Ebola assay, while orthoebolavirus-targeted tests detected infection; one RT-PCR was invalid in five samples, but genome sequencing confirmed BDBV. No approved Bundibugyo-specific vaccines or treatments exist; rapid decentralized molecular testing and near-real-time sequencing are emphasized. Findings published in Nature Medicine.

articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has spread to a sixth province, Bas-Uele, after a death in the provincial capital Buta. Since the outbreak was declared May 15, the virus has expanded from three to 54 health zones across six provinces: Ituri (epicenter), North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, South Kivu, and Bas-Uele. Bas-Uele borders the Central African Republic; Haut-Uélé borders South Sudan. Transmission remains active in five provinces; South Kivu has had no new cases for 76 days. The DRC government reports 2,128 deaths and 4,566 confirmed cases. WHO notes the virus began circulating in eastern DRC in February (some studies suggest January). The Bundibugyo strain has a 30–50% fatality rate, with no licensed vaccine or specific treatment. Uganda was declared Ebola-free on July 28 after 20 cases (15 imported).

articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in Mongbwalu, a gold-mining town in Ituri province, DRC, is hampered by severe water shortages and poor sanitation. articleHeadline: In Ituri, former combatants join the fight against Ebola with MONUSCO support
articleSummary: Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) in Ituri Province, DRC, is being tackled in Tchomia (65 km south of Bunia) by demobilized former combatants trained as community mobilizers. Thirty-two outreach workers—27 former combatants under the P-DDRCS—received training on prevention, early detection of suspected cases, and risk communication. They visit markets, town centers, restaurants, and the animal feed site to promote handwashing, rapid symptom identification, and prompt reporting to health authorities. A vocational training plan will soon reach 233 beneficiaries (87 former combatants and 146 community members, including 66 vulnerable women) to develop local processing of nutritious animal feed for fish farming, poultry, and other livestock. The initiative aims to reduce dependence on imports from Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda, strengthen livelihoods, and support community resilience during the Ebola response. MONUSCO DDR-S, with HPD and RAD ASBL, supports reintegration under the P-DDRCS framework.
